one_liner: MIT double-precision Stockham FFT library for x86 (SSE2/AVX/AVX2) whose upstream author claims it beats FFTW at 2^1 to 2^24.
what_it_does: OTFFT computes double-precision complex FFTs, real-to-complex FFTs, DCT-II and Bluestein FFTs of arbitrary length in 1-D only. The DEWETRON fork packages OK Ojisan's (Takuya Okahisa) upstream code, synced to version 11.5, as a CMake static library. Its public header exposes abstract ComplexFFT / RealFFT / RealDCT classes created through OTFFT::Factory::createComplexFFT(n), createRealFFT, createDCT and createBluesteinFFT, with fwd/fwd0/fwdu/fwdn and inv/inv0/invu/invn methods that select the normalization. The API is its own, not FFTW-compatible.
how_it_is_fast: It uses the self-sorting Stockham algorithm (no bit-reversal pass) in radix-4, -8 and -16 decimation-in-frequency and decimation-in-time variants, written as C++ templates over SSE2 (__m128d) and AVX/AVX2 (__m256d) complex arithmetic. Large power-of-two sizes use a six-step/eight-step (cache-blocked, transpose-based) algorithm, and other lengths use a mixed-radix kernel. A hard-coded table, copied from upstream's ffttune-generated setup, picks one of these seven kernels for each power of two up to 2^24. Above 2^15 points it runs OpenMP loops automatically unless built with DO_SINGLE_THREAD.
when_to_use: Double-precision 1-D complex or real FFTs on x86-64 desktops and servers where an MIT license matters and FFTW's GPL does not fit
Power-of-two lengths from 2 to 2^24, the range the upstream benchmark covers
Windows (MSVC) or Linux (GCC/Clang) products that need one binary for SSE2, AVX and AVX2 machines: the fork builds all three back-ends and picks one at run time with CPUID
Applications that also need DCT-II or arbitrary-length (Bluestein) transforms from the same small library
when_not_to_use: When you need a verified win over FFTW: no repository has numbers, and the only comparison is the upstream homepage (search snippet, not opened: OTFFT 11.6 vs FFTW 3.3.10 multi-threaded on a Surface Laptop 5 under WSL2, GCC 11.4.0, OTFFT taking 81% of FFTW's time at 2^10 and 89% at 2^11; FFTW planner flags unknown). This fork is at 11.5, not 11.6
Single precision, 2-D/3-D transforms, batched/strided (guru-style) plans, or wisdom: none exist
ARM, Apple Silicon or other non-x86 targets: kernels are SSE2/AVX intrinsics and dispatch uses x86 cpuid/xgetbv inline assembly; kfrlib/fft-benchmark lists it as x86 only
AVX-512 machines expecting 512-bit kernels: the build only compiles SSE2, AVX and AVX2 back-ends
Projects that need upkeep: the fork's last commit is 2022-08-17, and the kernel-selection table was tuned on the upstream author's machine with no ffttune tool in the fork to retune it

integration.dependencies: OpenMP (find_package(OpenMP REQUIRED) in the standalone build); Boost.Test only for the unit tests
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; CMake 3.0+; GCC, Clang, Intel C++ or MSVC (CI badges: Ubuntu 14.04 and 20.04, VS2013; a 2018 commit fixed the VS2017 build)
integration.platforms: x86 only; x86-64 gets SSE2, AVX and AVX2 back-ends chosen at run time by CPUID, 32-bit x86 builds only the SSE2 back-end
integration.thread_safety: Not formally documented. The README says to use FFT0/DCT0 with a caller-supplied work buffer in multi-threaded code and to create one Bluestein object per thread, so do not share one transform object across threads. The library itself spawns OpenMP threads for N >= 2^15.

gotchas: fwd() divides by N (forward normalization), unlike FFTW's unnormalized forward transform; use fwd0() for FFTW-style scaling. inv() is unnormalized, and the real inverse transforms destroy their input

The factory comment says complex, real and DCT lengths must be even (up to 2^30); only the Bluestein transform takes any length (up to 2^28). Non-power-of-two and above-2^24 lengths fall through to the mixed-radix kernel
Internal OpenMP parallelism above 2^15 points can oversubscribe cores when the caller already runs FFTs on several threads; define DO_SINGLE_THREAD to turn it off

The README examples (OTFFT::FFT fft(N), OTFFT::FFT0) do not match the public header, which only exports the Factory functions. The CPUID probe also runs xgetbv before checking the OSXSAVE bit, so it can fault with an invalid-instruction error on CPUs or VMs without XSAVE
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose OTFFT over PocketFFT or PFFFT only if you want x86 double-precision 1-D transforms with run-time AVX2/AVX/SSE2 dispatch under MIT and accept an unmaintained codebase; PocketFFT (N-D, any length, any arch) and KFR or VectorFFT (published wins over FFTW/MKL) are the better-documented choices.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing measured was opened. The upstream homepage (egress-blocked here; seen only through a search snippet) reports OTFFT 11.6 faster than multi-threaded FFTW 3.3.10 at every power of two from 2^1 to 2^24 on a Surface Laptop 5 (10 cores/12 threads, WSL2 Ubuntu 22.04, GCC 11.4.0). The snippet gives two ratios, 81% of FFTW's time at 2^10 and 89% at 2^11. The upstream benchmark sources (fftbench with an FFTW3 wrapper) exist, but their FFTW planner flags were not seen.
status_note: Abandoned: the fork has 38 commits, the last a 2022-08-17 upstream sync to 11.5, and no open issues. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor as a CMake static library, with unit tests and a GitHub Actions build.
